full_judgment:
"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 14-11-2007 (Annexure-G) passed by the Waqf Administration (respondent No.1) in EC Case No. 186, Haji Kala Mia Chowdhury Waqf Estate Chittagong by accepting the registered deed of agreement dated 27-2-1983 (Annexure-B) made in between Syed Ahmed Khan and Mahmud Ali Khan and thereby partitioned the Waqf Property and created two separate Waqf Estate with two separate enrolment certificate No. EC 186(Ka) and EC 186(Kha) and appointment of two Mutwallies in respect of divided estate in reviewing his won judgment and order dated 20-7-2005 (Annexure-D) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect." 

 3. The averments figured leading to the Rule in both the petitions are common in nature, which are as under: The predecessor of the petitioners and the respondent No.2 and 3 namely Haji Kala Miah Chowdhury made an Waqf Estate by registered deed dated 20-11-1934 which was enrolled in the office of Administrator of Waqf bearing EC No. 186 and dedicated his entire immovable property for religious/ charitable purpose as well as for maintenance of the family. The status of the Waqf was a "Waqf-e-Lillah and Alal-Awlad" under certain terms and conditions as contained in the registered Waqf deed. The said waqf deed incorporated the terms as to the appointment of Mutwalli and as per terms the Wakif himself became the First Mutwalli and made provisions that after his death, elder son Syed Ahmed Khan would be the Mutwalli and thereafter his second son Mahmud Ali Khan would be the Mutwalli each by rotation for there years in turn and when one son would act as Mutwalli another son would act as 'Nayeb-e-Mutwall'. It was clearly mentioned in the deed itself that there would be no joint Mutwalliship at the same time, in case of death of one son the surviving son would act as Mutwalli till his death. On the death of his two sons their legal heirs as per seniority and competence would be the Mutwalli by rotation for three years. 

 15. We have to discuss some cases having bearing on the issue. In the case of Abdul Sobhan Bhuiya vs Wasin Bhuiya, 1 DLR 164 wherein it was held: "Apart from this, it is now settled law that even a wakif, after he has created a wakf and made provision for the appointment of mutawalli, has no power to alter the arrangement and remove the mutawalli appointed by him, unless he reserves such powers at the time he creates the wakf, vide the case of Siddiq Ahmed Choudhury vs Syed Ahmed Choudhury reported in 49 CWN page 311." 

 17. In case of Mirza Iftikhar Ali vs Mirza Akbar Ali reported in 6 DLR (FC) 135, it was held that mode of succession to the office of Mutawalliship can be said to be indicated in a Waqf-deed, only when by following that mode one can find out a specific person who is to succeed the last Mutawalli. A vague direction in the deed of Wakf which cannot lead to the appointment of definite person as a successor cannot be regarded as a provision relating to the mode of succession.
